degraded.credentials: The cluster refused the credential. Check the username, password and SASL mechanism: a broker that rejects authentication may close the connection instead of explaining, so a wrong mechanism looks the same as a wrong password.
degraded.forbidden: The credential was accepted but is not allowed to describe the cluster. That is fixed with an ACL on the broker, not in this form.
degraded.timeout: The cluster accepted the connection and did not answer in time.
degraded.unreachable: Nothing usable answered at this address. Check the bootstrap servers, and whether the listener expects TLS or a security protocol this connection is not using.
degraded.accessControl: This cluster runs without an authorizer, so it enforces no ACLs and every access-control call answers SECURITY_DISABLED.

caveat.browseAltersQueue: Browsing alters the queue: messages are requeued but come back flagged redelivered, and concurrent consumers see the gap.

degraded.managementPlugin: The management API answered 404: nothing is mounted at that address. Check that the management plugin is enabled and that the address points at the management port.
degraded.credentials: The username or password was rejected (the management API answered 401). Check the credentials in the connection settings.
degraded.forbidden: The credentials are valid, but this user has no management tag and cannot read the management API (403). Give it the management tag or higher.
degraded.timeout: Timed out reaching the management API. Check the broker is reachable, or raise the timeout in the connection settings.
degraded.unreachable: Cannot reach the management API. Check the address and port, and that the management plugin is enabled - with it off nothing listens on the management port at all, which looks the same from here as a wrong address.
degraded.amqpAccessRefused: The management API works but the AMQP connection was refused: this user has no permission on the virtual host. Browsing and publishing are unavailable; the admin views are not affected.
degraded.amqpTimeout: Timed out reaching the AMQP port. Check the address and port, and that nothing is filtering it.
degraded.amqpUnreachable: Cannot reach the AMQP port. The admin views still work, but browsing and publishing do not - check the AMQP address and port.
degraded.replicationPlugin: The shovel and federation plugins are not enabled on this broker, so the cross-broker pages have nothing to read. That is a deployment choice rather than a failure - enable them with rabbitmq-plugins enable rabbitmq_shovel rabbitmq_shovel_management.
degraded.streamPlugin: The broker does not have the rabbitmq_stream_management plugin enabled. A stream queue still works over AMQP; only its stream protocol clients are invisible.

routing.title: Exchanges & bindings
routing.empty: No bindings in this virtual host

degraded.credentials: The cluster rejected the token. Check that it has not expired, and that it was issued by the authentication provider this cluster trusts.
degraded.forbidden: The token was accepted but its role has no permission on this tenant. That is fixed with a grant on the cluster, not in this form.
degraded.tenantMissing: The cluster answered, and the tenant this connection is scoped to is not on it. Check the tenant name, or create it.
degraded.timeout: The admin API accepted the connection and did not answer in time.
degraded.unreachable: Nothing answered at the admin API address. Check the address, and whether the web service expects HTTPS.
degraded.dataPlaneUnreachable: The admin API answers and the broker's binary port does not, so this connection can read but not publish. Check the service URL and whether that port is reachable from here.
degraded.loadReport: This cluster's load manager publishes no figures, so brokers report no rates or resource usage. NoopLoadManager - the standalone default - is the usual reason; a clustered deployment normally runs ModularLoadManagerImpl.

degraded.credentials: The server refused the credential. Check the username and password: before Redis 6 there are no users and the password alone is the credential, so an unexpected username fails against a server that is otherwise reachable.
degraded.credentialsNotRequired: The server has no password set and refused the one this connection sent. Clear the password field rather than correcting it.
degraded.forbidden: The credential was accepted but its ACL does not allow this command. That is fixed with ACL SETUSER on the server, not in this form.
degraded.loading: The server is reading its dataset back into memory and is not answering yet. It recovers on its own; nothing here needs changing.
degraded.timeout: The server accepted the connection and did not answer in time.
degraded.unreachable: Nothing usable answered at this address. A TLS-only server reached without TLS looks the same from here, so check that setting as well as the address.

degraded.sysRefused: The broker refused a subscription to its $SYS tree. That is a rule rather than a fault — EMQX denies it to any client that is not local — so the figures come from its management API instead where there is one. To read $SYS, allow the subscription in the broker's authorisation.
degraded.sysSilent: The broker took the subscription and publishes no $SYS tree at all. There is nothing to configure: this broker simply does not report on itself, and the pages that would read it stay empty.
degraded.managementAbsent: This connection names no management API, and MQTT itself cannot say who is connected — there is no such request in the protocol. Mosquitto has no such API at all; EMQX and its peers do, and its address goes in the connection's advanced settings.
degraded.managementUnreachable: The management API named on this connection did not answer. The address and port are in the connection's advanced settings; the broker's own MQTT port is a different one.
degraded.managementCredentials: The management API refused the API key. Check the key and secret in the connection's advanced settings — on EMQX they are created in its dashboard under API keys, and are not the dashboard login.
degraded.managementUnknown: Something answered at that address and it was not this broker's management API. The address is most likely off by a port, or a proxy is in front of a broker that has no such API.

degraded.jetstreamDisabled: This server was started without JetStream, so it stores nothing: there are no streams, no consumers and no message history to read. Start the server with --jetstream, or point this connection at one that already runs it.
degraded.jetstreamNoAccount: The server runs JetStream and this account may not use it. Nothing needs to change about how the server was started — add a jetstream block to the account in the server's configuration, or connect as one that already has one.
degraded.monitorAbsent: This connection names no monitoring endpoint, and the protocol itself cannot say what a server is doing — there is no such request in NATS. The endpoint is served on port 8222 when the server is started with -m; its address goes in the connection's advanced settings.
degraded.monitorUnreachable: The monitoring endpoint named on this connection did not answer. Check the address and port in the connection's advanced settings, and that the server was started with -m — the client port is a different one.
degraded.systemAbsent: This connection carries no system-account credentials, so the cluster can only be asked about the one server the monitoring endpoint belongs to. The system account is a separate account with its own user; its credentials go in the connection's advanced settings.
degraded.systemForbidden: The system-account credentials on this connection were refused. An ordinary account cannot reach $SYS however valid it is — these have to be a user inside the account named by system_account in the server's configuration.

degraded.amqpAbsent: This connection names no AMQP address, so there is no open socket to follow a destination on. Everything else works without one — browsing and sending both go through the console. Add the broker's AMQP acceptor to this connection to turn live following on.
degraded.amqpUnreachable: The AMQP address was configured and nothing answered on it. Check that the broker declares an AMQP acceptor and that it is reachable from here: on Classic it is a transportConnector in activemq.xml, on Artemis an acceptor in broker.xml.
degraded.amqpForbidden: The broker answered on AMQP and turned these credentials away. The console and the broker authenticate against different realms, so an account that opens the console need not open a connection — give this connection its own AMQP credentials.

caveat.browseCapped: Classic returns at most maxBrowsePageSize messages per browse, 400 by default, however deep the destination is. The page shows what the broker sent — raise the limit in the destination's policy entry to see further.

degraded.lookupdAbsent: This connection names no nsqlookupd, so there is no discovery tier to describe. Everything else works without one — a single-node NSQ has none at all. Add the nsqlookupd addresses to this connection to see which daemons it is advertising and which topics it knows.

caveat.receiveHides: Browsing goes through ReceiveMessage, which is the same call a consumer makes: what it reads is hidden from other consumers until this app hands it back, and its receive count goes up for good. On a queue with a redrive policy, that counts towards being dead-lettered.

degraded.lagInMonitoring: A subscription's backlog is num_undelivered_messages, which is a Cloud Monitoring metric rather than a field on the subscription — no call in the Pub/Sub API reports it. Read it in Cloud Monitoring, or give the subscription a dead-letter topic so what is failing is somewhere countable.

caveat.pullDelivers: Browsing goes through Pull, which is the same call a consumer makes: what it reads is held away from other consumers until this app hands it back, and its delivery attempt goes up for good. On a subscription with a dead-letter topic, that counts towards being moved there.

degraded.countsNotInEmulator: The Service Bus emulator reports no message counts: a queue's and a topic's description carry no CountDetails element at all, and a subscription's carries one the SDK cannot read. Depths and backlogs are blank here and only here — a real namespace reports both.

rabbitmq.rebalanceDesc: Spreads quorum queue leaders back across the nodes. They pile up on whichever node was available when each queue was declared, especially after a rolling restart, and the broker does not spread them on its own.

position.idRequired: Enter the entry id to move to.

nats.ackNoneHint: Nothing is acknowledged, so nothing is ever redelivered — a message a consumer drops is simply gone from its point of view.
nats.ackWaitHint: How long the server waits before handing an unacknowledged message to somebody else. Empty means 30 seconds.
nats.maxDeliverHint: After the last attempt the message is not moved anywhere — JetStream has no dead-letter queue. It stops being redelivered and only an advisory says so.
nats.maxAckPendingHint: How much unacknowledged work the server will hand out before it stops.
nats.filterHint: Which of the stream's subjects this consumer takes. Empty takes all of them; several may be given.
nats.wholeStream: Takes every subject in the stream.
nats.deliverSubjectHint: Filling this in makes it a push consumer: the server sends to that subject instead of waiting to be asked. Leave it empty for the ordinary pull kind.
nats.deliverGroupHint: Shares the delivered messages between everything listening on that subject under this group name.
nats.durableHint: A durable consumer keeps its position when nothing is using it. An ephemeral one is cleaned up, taking that position with it.
nats.name: Name
nats.nameHint: Not a subject: a consumer name cannot contain a dot, a wildcard or a space.

rocketmq.bodyTruncated: Body too large — showing the first {{shown}} KB of {{total}} KB. The cut-off is a setting.

nats.title: Messages
nats.subtitle: Browse what a stream is holding
nats.subject: Subject
nats.startHere: Pick a stream and search. Nothing is read until you ask — a browse walks the stream, and doing it on its own would re-read one nobody is looking at.
nats.noMatches: No message in that stream matched.
nats.headerFilterNote: JetStream narrows by subject and by nothing else, so the header filter runs here after the messages arrive. It saves reading, not fetching.
nats.emptyBody: This message has no payload. That is ordinary in NATS — a subject on its own is a signal, and request/reply uses empty messages routinely.

rocketmq.hint: A redelivery is written under a new MsgId; the original is kept
rocketmq.risky: High-risk · written to the audit log
rocketmq.confirmBody: They are rewritten under a new MsgId to {{topic}} for {{group}} to consume normally; the originals stay in the dead-letter queue and can be deleted later.
rocketmq.liveSubtitle: Pick a consumer group to see its retry and dead-letter queues
rocketmq.pickGroupHint: Retry and dead-letter queues are kept per consumer group, so one has to be named before there is anything to read.
rocketmq.noDlq: This group has no dead letters

redis.title: Pending entries
redis.subtitle: Redis moves nothing aside; what is not acknowledged stays owed to the consumer that was handed it
redis.noGroups: No consumer group was found, so nothing is owed to anyone.
redis.nothingPending: This group has nothing outstanding: every entry it was handed has been acknowledged.
redis.nothingIdle: Nothing has been sitting that long. Lower the threshold to see work still in flight.
redis.bulkHint: Claiming moves the entries to another consumer. Acknowledging settles them without anything having processed them.
redis.ackHint: This settles them without anything having processed them. The entries stay in the stream and this group never reads them again, and nothing afterwards distinguishes that from work that was done. Redis has no undo.
redis.ackNone: None of those were still owed; somebody settled them first.

claim.title: Claim {{count}} entries
claim.consumerHint: It need not exist yet: claiming creates it, which is how a replacement takes over from a dead worker.
claim.consumerRequired: Enter the consumer to move the entries to.
claim.minIdleHint: The guard against taking work from a consumer that is simply busy. Without it both would believe they own the same entry.
claim.minIdleZero: Zero moves the entries whatever their idle time. Right when the consumer is known to be gone; wrong whenever it is merely busy.
claim.idleInvalid: The idle threshold must be a whole number of minutes.
claim.autoHint: This walks the pending list rather than a selection, and moves everything past the threshold.
claim.none: Nothing moved: every entry had been touched more recently than the threshold allows.
claim.lost: {{count}} entries were owed but no longer in the stream. They were dropped from the pending list rather than moved: that work is gone.

pulsar.title: Dead letters
pulsar.subtitle: Subscription settle-sub · order-created-settle-sub-DLQ · 8 messages
pulsar.rule: maxRedeliverCount=5 · past that it goes to the DLQ
pulsar.hint: Discarding acks it on the DLQ · the source subscription is untouched
pulsar.none: No topic in this namespace follows the dead-letter naming convention.
pulsar.conventionNote: Found by name: a consumer with a DLQ policy republishes to <topic>-<subscription>-DLQ. Pulsar records no link on the broker.
pulsar.orphanBanner: {{count}} of these have no origin topic left: nothing will ever drain them, and nothing points at them any more.

rabbitmq.title: Dead letters
rabbitmq.subtitle: {{count}} queues are receiving dead letters
rabbitmq.browseWarn: Reading a dead-letter queue is the same browse as any other: messages are taken and put back, and come back flagged redelivered.
rabbitmq.none: No queue in this virtual host declares a dead-letter exchange
rabbitmq.pressFetch: Take a batch to see what is in it
rabbitmq.noSources: Nothing dead-letters here - the queue that did may have been deleted or reconfigured
rabbitmq.dropDesc: Takes up to {{count}} from the head and acknowledges them. Acknowledging removes them from the broker with no dead-lettering and no copy anywhere. There is no undo.

producer.noteHeaders: Headers go in the shared custom-properties block · with no key the partitioner decides
producer.noteConfirm: Confirm mode returns ack/nack · mandatory returns anything it cannot route
producer.noteProps: Properties go in the shared block · a failed schema check rejects the send
producer.noteXadd: * generates the ID · maxlen ~ trims approximately, which is faster

producer.notWired: This protocol is not wired up yet; only RocketMQ connections can send
producer.noSends: Nothing sent in this session yet
producer.notJson: The body is not valid JSON, so it cannot be formatted

clients.title: Who is publishing
clients.hint: Brokers index connections by producer group and offer no call that lists the groups, so the name has to be typed.
clients.none: No producer connected under this group

producer.resetHint: Clears the form and forgets what this topic had saved
producer.draftRestored: Restored what was last sent to this topic

rabbitmq.title: Publish
rabbitmq.subtitle: Send to an exchange or straight to a queue, and wait for the broker

addressingHint.queue: Through the default exchange with the queue's name as the routing key - which is what publishing to a queue means in AMQP
addressingHint.exchange: To a named exchange, which decides from the routing key which queues receive it

rabbitmq.persistentHint: Off, the message lives in memory only and is lost when the node restarts - even on a durable queue
rabbitmq.mandatoryHint: Off, a message no queue receives is dropped by the broker and still confirmed, so this console would report the loss as a success
rabbitmq.countHint: Sends the same message repeatedly, for load or for filling a queue. Each waits for its own confirm.
rabbitmq.headersHint: One per line, as kind=order. A headers exchange matches on exactly these.
rabbitmq.expirationHint: Milliseconds. A per-message TTL, after which it is dropped or dead-lettered.
rabbitmq.priorityHint: Only honoured on a queue declared with x-max-priority; ignored otherwise

kafka.title: Send
kafka.subtitle: Write one record, or many, and be told where it landed
kafka.acksNoneWarning: With acks=none the cluster is never asked, so a reported success is not evidence the record was kept and there are no coordinates to read it back by.
kafka.keyHint: off sends a record with no key at all, which Kafka spreads across partitions

invalid.partitionInvalid: A partition is a whole number, or blank to let the key decide
invalid.headerLine: Each header is one key=value per line

redis.subtitle: Write an entry to a stream
redis.streamHint: This will not create a stream. A mistyped key would otherwise become a new one holding a single test entry.
redis.streamRequired: Choose a stream to write to.
redis.noStreams: The key pattern found no stream to write to. Create one on the stream page first.
redis.fieldsHint: The order is kept. Reading a stream loses it - the client hands fields back unordered - so this is the only place it survives.
redis.fieldRequired: An entry needs at least one named field.
redis.entryIdHint: Leave empty to let the server assign one from its clock, which is what keeps a stream ordered.
redis.idWithCount: An explicit id can only be used once. Send a single copy, or let the server assign ids.
redis.countHint: Writes the same entry this many times, each with its own id.
redis.countRequired: Enter how many copies to write.
redis.countInvalid: The number of copies must be a whole number of at least one.

mqtt.retainHint: keeps this as the topic's last known value until something overwrites it
mqtt.topicWildcard: A topic to publish to cannot contain + or #, which are subscription wildcards
mqtt.expiryInvalid: Message expiry must be a number of seconds
mqtt.propertyLine: Every user property must be name=value
mqtt.needsFive: These properties are MQTT 5.0 only and this connection is 3.1.1

pulsar.title: Send
pulsar.keyHint: What the broker partitions and compacts by.
pulsar.orderingKeyHint: Orders delivery independently of the key, for Key_Shared subscriptions.
pulsar.propertiesHint: One name=value per line. Pulsar has no tag; this is where one goes, and the messages page filters on it.
pulsar.delayHint: The broker holds the message and delivers when the time comes. 0 sends now.
pulsar.countHint: The same message, repeated. Capped at 1000.
pulsar.noPublishers: Nothing is publishing to this topic right now.
pulsar.delayInvalid: The delay must be a whole number of seconds
pulsar.countTooLarge: A single send is capped at 1000 messages

nats.title: Publish
nats.subtitle: Send a message on a subject
nats.subject: Subject
nats.subjectHint: An address, not a pattern. A wildcard here would match nothing: the server would accept it, deliver to nobody, and report success.
nats.countHint: Sends the same message this many times, up to 1000.
nats.payloadHint: Sent as it is. An empty payload is ordinary in NATS — a subject on its own is a signal.
nats.headersHint: One per line, written name: value. NATS carries headers natively, so nothing has to be packed into the body.
nats.persist: Wait for a stream to store it
nats.persistOn: The send is acknowledged by whichever stream captures the subject, and comes back with the sequence it landed at. It fails if no stream captures it.
nats.persistOff: A core send: it reaches whoever is listening at that instant and is forgotten. The server acknowledges nothing, which is the protocol rather than a fault.
nats.expectStreamHint: Refuses the send unless that stream is the one capturing the subject — the guard against a typo landing somewhere else.
nats.dedupIdHint: A second message carrying the same id inside the stream's duplicate window is accepted and not stored.
nats.replyHint: Turns the send into a request. Nobody listening and nobody answering in time are reported apart, because they are fixed in different places.
nats.noAcknowledgement: no acknowledgement — core NATS gives none
nats.duplicate: recognised as a duplicate and not stored again

error.subjectIsPattern: That is a pattern rather than an address. A wildcard subscribes; it does not publish — the server would accept this, match nothing, and report success.
error.subjectInvalid: That is not a valid subject: it cannot contain spaces or an empty token.
error.countInvalid: Repeat has to be a whole number between 1 and 1000.
error.waitInvalid: The reply timeout has to be a positive number of milliseconds.
error.requestCannotRepeat: A request expects one answer, so it cannot be repeated.
error.expectNeedsPersist: There is nothing to check a stream against on a core send. Turn on waiting for a stream first.
error.dedupNeedsPersist: Deduplication happens in the stream, so it means nothing on a core send.
error.headersInvalid: Each header goes on its own line, written name: value.

mqtt.startToSee: Subscribe to a filter to see messages
mqtt.sessionDown: The session dropped. Nothing is arriving until it reconnects.
mqtt.dropped: {{count}} messages were dropped: the stream is arriving faster than this page reads it.
mqtt.noHistory: MQTT stores no history. {{count}} messages have arrived since this subscription started, and closing the page loses them.

rabbitmq.subtitle: {{count}} of them - queues, exchanges, bindings, policies and permissions all live inside one and none is visible from another
rabbitmq.none: No virtual hosts could be read
rabbitmq.name: Name
rabbitmq.nameHint: Cannot be renamed afterwards - a rename is a new virtual host
rabbitmq.nameFixed: The name is the identity and cannot change
rabbitmq.defaultQueueTypeHint: What a queue declared here without a type becomes. Most client libraries declare without one, so whatever is chosen here is what most queues will be.
rabbitmq.tagsHint: Comma separated, for people; the broker does nothing with them
rabbitmq.tracingHint: Copies every message through this virtual host to a log exchange. It is expensive and is meant for minutes of diagnosis, not to be left on.
rabbitmq.limitHint: Empty means no limit - which is not the same as 0, and 0 allows none at all
rabbitmq.deleteDesc: Its queues, {{count}} messages, exchanges, bindings, policies and permissions go with it. There is no undo.
rabbitmq.deleteFailed: Could not delete the virtual host

pulsar.title: Namespaces
pulsar.name: Name
pulsar.nameHint: Created under this connection's tenant. Letters, digits, dots, hyphens and underscores.
pulsar.nameSlash: A namespace name cannot contain a slash; the tenant is set by the connection
pulsar.nameInvalid: Only letters, digits, dots, hyphens and underscores
pulsar.limitsHint: Clearing a field hands the limit back to the broker's own default, which is not the same as setting it to zero.
pulsar.retentionNote: Pulsar stores the retention pair as one policy, so clearing either half clears both.
pulsar.deleteBody: {{name}} is removed. Pulsar refuses while it still holds topics.

nats.title: Accounts
nats.subtitle: The isolation boundaries on this cluster
nats.readOnly: Accounts come from the server's configuration file, or from a JWT signed with nsc — there is no request that creates one.
nats.oneServer: These figures are from the one server the monitoring endpoint belongs to.
nats.noJetStream: This account has no JetStream. It can publish and subscribe; nothing it sends is stored.

rabbitmq.title: Policies
rabbitmq.subtitle: A queue's arguments are fixed once declared; a policy is the only way to change a running one
rabbitmq.name: Name
rabbitmq.nameFixed: The name is the identity; a rename is a new policy
rabbitmq.patternHint: A regular expression matched against queue or exchange names. ^order\\. matches everything starting with order.
rabbitmq.applyToHint: A definition meant for quorum queues applied to all queues is rejected on every classic queue it matches, and the broker reports that per queue rather than when the policy is saved
rabbitmq.priorityHint: Only one policy applies to a given queue - the highest-priority match. Policies do not merge.
rabbitmq.priorityNote: Only the highest-priority matching policy applies. The others have no effect at all; they are not merged.
rabbitmq.operatorHint: Operator policies are set by whoever runs the broker; where both set the same key, the more restrictive value wins
rabbitmq.definitionInvalid: The definition is not valid JSON
rabbitmq.definitionNotObject: The definition must be a JSON object
rabbitmq.definitionEmpty: The definition is empty - this policy would match queues and change nothing about them
rabbitmq.deleteDesc: Every queue matched by {{pattern}} reverts to whatever it was declared with, immediately and with no warning from the broker.
rabbitmq.parameterHint: Configuration the broker stores for its plugins. Shovels and federation upstreams live here - read and delete only, because a parameter's shape belongs to whichever plugin owns it and nothing here can validate one.
rabbitmq.deleteParameterDesc: It belongs to the {{component}} component, whose configuration it is.

rabbitmq.title: Definitions
rabbitmq.subtitle: The whole topology as one JSON document - RabbitMQ's only backup of anything but messages
rabbitmq.brokerScopeHint: Includes every user and permission, and every user's password hash - treat the file as a credential
rabbitmq.vhostScopeHint: Only this virtual host's queues, exchanges, bindings, policies and parameters. No users or permissions: those are broker-wide.
rabbitmq.exportHint: Written as a JSON file. It is what a cluster is rebuilt from.
rabbitmq.importHint: Choose a file, see what is in it, then decide whether to apply it.
rabbitmq.empty: There is nothing in this file
rabbitmq.additiveWarn: Importing adds and overwrites; it does not synchronise. Anything named in the document is created or overwritten, and anything on the broker the document does not mention is left exactly as it is - so this cannot make a cluster match a file, only put the file's contents into it.
rabbitmq.importDesc: Creates or overwrites {{count}} objects. A queue, exchange, policy or user of the same name is replaced by the file's version, and there is no undo.

rabbitmq.title: Replication
rabbitmq.subtitle: Shovels and federation - the two ways messages move between brokers
rabbitmq.shovelHint: A shovel moves messages from somewhere to somewhere and is done. Its definition carries the other broker's credentials in a URI, so these are read and delete only - one is declared where the rest of a deployment is.
rabbitmq.federationHint: Federation keeps two brokers' exchanges or queues in step continuously. An upstream is configuration; the link is the connection.
rabbitmq.redacted: The password was removed before this left the broker
rabbitmq.deleteShovelDesc: It stops moving messages at once. Anything not yet moved stays in the source queue; nothing is lost.
rabbitmq.deleteUpstreamDesc: Its links close and the two brokers stop keeping each other in step.

kafka.title: Quotas
kafka.subtitle: What the cluster will let one client do, in total
kafka.name: Name
kafka.isDefaultHint: every client of this type with no quota of its own
kafka.deleteBody: Every limit on this entity is cleared. Clients it covered fall back to the default for their type, or to no limit at all if there is none.
kafka.zeroNote: A blank field leaves a limit alone. A zero is a real quota that throttles the client to nothing, so it is not the way to say “no limit”.
kafka.empty: This cluster enforces no client quotas. Every client can use as much of it as it asks for.

invalid.entityRequired: Pick what the quota applies to
invalid.nameRequired: Enter a name, or make it the default
invalid.duplicateType: Each dimension can only appear once
invalid.ipCombination: An IP quota throttles connections before anyone authenticates, so it cannot be combined with a user or client id
invalid.limitInvalid: A limit is a number and cannot be negative

redis.title: Clients
redis.subtitle: The connections open against this server
redis.search: Search by address, name, user or command…
redis.none: Nothing is connected, which cannot include this connection - try refreshing.
redis.closeHint: The client is disconnected immediately. A well-written one reconnects; anything mid-command loses that command's reply.
redis.closeSelf: This is the connection this page is using. Closing it disconnects the console, and the tab will need reconnecting.

nats.title: Connections
nats.subtitle: Clients the cluster is holding
nats.search: Search a client, address or subject
nats.noClients: Nothing is connected but this app.
nats.publishesOnly: This connection subscribes to nothing — it only publishes.
nats.closeDescription: The server {{server}} drops the socket. Most NATS libraries reconnect on their own within a second, so this interrupts the client rather than stopping it — to keep it away, stop the application.
nats.cannotClose: Read through the monitoring endpoint, which is read-only. Add system-account credentials to the connection to disconnect clients.

nats.title: Subjects
nats.subtitle: Watch messages as they go past
nats.notStarted: Name one or more subjects and start. Wildcards work here — this is a subscription, not an address.
nats.waiting: Listening. Nothing has been published on those subjects yet.
nats.disconnected: The connection dropped, so nothing is being received. It will resume on its own when the connection comes back.

destinations.name: Destination
destinations.browseCapped: Deeper than one browse returns. Classic stops at {{cap}} messages per browse however deep the destination is; the message page shows what the broker sent.

note.classic: ActiveMQ Classic. A queue and a topic live in separate MBean trees, and advisory topics are hidden — the broker publishes one per destination per event.
note.artemis: ActiveMQ Artemis. A row is an address: anycast makes it a queue, multicast a topic, and a multicast address's queues are its durable subscriptions rather than destinations of their own.

destinations.kindHint: A queue and a topic can share a name — on Classic they are different objects in different trees — so this cannot be inferred.
destinations.purgeDesc: Discards {{count}} messages. There is no undo. On a topic this empties every subscription under it.
destinations.deleteDesc: Removes the destination and everything it holds. There is no undo.
destinations.moveHint: The destination messages are moved into. ActiveMQ moves by name — there is no exchange or routing key in between.

subscriptions.name: Subscription
subscriptions.topicHint: Only a topic can hold a durable subscription. A queue's consumers are connections — no name, no stored position, gone when the socket closes.
subscriptions.clientIdHint: Classic identifies a durable subscription by the client that registered it, together with the subscription's own name.
subscriptions.selectorHint: A JMS selector expression, or empty for everything. It is fixed when the subscription is created.
subscriptions.deleteDesc: Discards the {{count}} messages the broker is still holding for it. There is no undo.
subscriptions.note: A subscription with nothing attached is not a fault — the broker is holding messages for a client that has gone away, which is what durable means.

messages.largeBody: A large message's body is stored outside the journal and is not part of a browse result. What is shown elsewhere on this page is the message's headers, which are.
messages.capped: This destination is deeper than one browse returns. Classic stops at 400 messages per browse whatever the depth, and the limit is not readable over JMX — what is listed is what the broker sent.

dlq.name: Destination
dlq.retryDesc: Sends {{count}} messages back to the destinations they originally failed on. Anything that fails again comes back here.
dlq.retryNote: Each message goes back to the destination it failed on, not onto a separate retry path. Both products retry the whole destination — neither takes a selector.
dlq.noSourcesClassic: Classic decides where a dead letter goes by a broker-wide policy and keeps no record of what fed this destination. Naming the sources from the destination list would be a guess.
dlq.noSourcesArtemis: Nothing points here any more. Whatever is holding will stay: no queue names this address, so it will never receive anything again.

producer.title: Send a message
producer.artemisQueuesOnly: Artemis sends through a queue. A multicast address has no queue of its own to send through, so topics are not listed here.
producer.textOnly: Text only. Both products' send operations take a string, so a binary body needs the AMQP tier.
producer.headersHint: One key: value per line. They arrive as string properties a selector can match.
producer.badHeader: Not a key/value pair: {{line}}. Sent as-is it becomes a property named after the whole line.
producer.persistentHint: Whether the message survives a broker restart.
producer.persistentClassic: Classic's send operation has no delivery-mode parameter — the destination's own policy decides, so this switch would do nothing here.
producer.countHint: Each copy is its own call, sent as one batch. Capped at 500.

cluster.name: Broker
cluster.bridgeNote: A broker this one forwards to. The link is configured here and the broker at the other end answers on its own console, which this connection cannot reach — so its state is genuinely unknown rather than assumed.
cluster.note: One broker, and the links it declares. A JMS broker is a unit — destinations live on the one that owns them — so clustering here is a bridge between brokers rather than nodes sharing a namespace. No rate is shown anywhere: both products keep cumulative counters and nothing else.

clients.search: Filter by peer, user or client id
clients.closeDesc: Closes the socket. A client that reconnects on its own will be back within seconds.
clients.sessionNote: Sessions are not channels. A channel has its own prefetch and flow control and can be closed on its own; a JMS session is a unit of work inside the connection and has none of that, which is why it is a column here rather than a page.

overview.subtitle: {{product}} {{version}}
overview.note: No rate is shown. Both products keep cumulative enqueue and dequeue counters and report no rate at all, and dividing two samples of a counter would be this app's arithmetic printed as the broker's figure.

subscribe.waiting: Listening. Nothing has been published to this topic yet.
subscribe.notStarted: Choose a topic and start watching.
subscribe.note: Topics only. A JMS consumer consumes, so attaching one to a queue would take its messages — the message page browses instead, which takes nothing. Nothing here is stored: a message published before this stream started was never anywhere this page could find it.

topics.name: Topic
topics.heldPaused: {{count}} messages are sitting in the topic because it is paused. Nothing is copied into a channel while a topic is paused, and publishing still works — so this number grows until the pause is lifted.
topics.heldNoChannel: {{count}} messages are sitting in the topic because nothing has subscribed to it. nsqd copies a message into every channel as it arrives, and a topic with no channel holds them instead — the first channel created takes the lot.
topics.note: One row per topic, however many nsqd carry it. Depth can exceed the message count: nsqd copies each message into every channel, so a topic with two channels holds two copies of everything. Neither figure is a rate — nsqd counts since it started and reports no rate at all.
topics.nameHint: Letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore, up to 64 characters. It is created on every nsqd in this connection, so a producer reaching any of them finds it already there.
topics.nameEphemeral: An ephemeral topic keeps nothing on disk and is deleted the moment its last client disconnects. Drop the #ephemeral suffix for a topic that outlives its consumers.

nameProblem.tooLong: nsqd refuses a name longer than 64 characters, and the #ephemeral suffix counts towards that.
nameProblem.charset: nsqd accepts letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore only, with an optional #ephemeral suffix.

topics.pauseFailed: Could not change the pause state
topics.emptyDesc: {{count}} messages are discarded, from the topic and from every channel under it. There is no undo.
topics.deleteDesc: The topic, its channels and everything they hold go, on every nsqd and in the discovery tier. There is no undo.

channels.name: Channel
channels.topicHint: The topic this channel reads. It has to exist already — a channel is created on the daemons carrying its topic, and there are none for a topic that is not there.
channels.nameHint: Letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore, up to 64 characters. There is no starting position: on a topic that already has a channel it begins at nothing, and on one that has none it takes the queue the topic has been holding.
channels.nameEphemeral: An ephemeral channel is deleted the moment its last consumer disconnects, and its backlog goes with it. Drop the #ephemeral suffix for a channel that keeps messages while nothing is reading.
channels.pauseFailed: Could not change the pause state
channels.emptyDesc: {{count}} messages are discarded from this channel. The topic and its other channels keep their own copies. There is no undo.
channels.deleteDesc: The channel and its backlog go, on every nsqd carrying {{topic}} and in the discovery tier. Messages already published reach it nowhere else. There is no undo.
channels.stalled: {{count}} messages are waiting because this channel is paused. Its consumers are connected and asking for work; nsqd is sending none until the pause is lifted.
channels.note: A channel is this family's consumer group: every channel under a topic receives a copy of every message, and its depth is the backlog. There is no offset behind that depth, so nothing here moves a read position — a backlog is consumed or emptied, and there is no third way. In flight and deferred sit outside it.

producer.subtitle: One body, to one nsqd
producer.title: Send
producer.topicHint: Publishing to a topic that does not exist creates it, on the daemon that took the message and nowhere else — so a name typed wrong leaves a topic behind rather than failing.
producer.topicRequired: Choose a topic to publish to.
producer.bodyHint: An NSQ message is bytes. There is no key, no header table and no property map anywhere in the protocol, so anything a consumer needs to know goes in here.
producer.nodeHint: The daemon that takes the message is the one holding it. A consumer attached to another sees it only if it also finds this one through nsqlookupd.
producer.delayHint: Held back from the channels for this long. nsqd caps it at its --max-req-timeout, {{max}} seconds by default, and refuses anything longer — the limit is not readable over the API, so this is the default rather than your daemon's.
producer.countHint: Sends the same body this many times, up to {{max}}, as one batch.
producer.countRange: Send between 1 and 1000 messages at a time.
producer.oneAtATime: These {{count}} go one request at a time rather than as a batch: /mpub separates messages with a newline and ignores a delay outright.
producer.delayCeiling: Past nsqd's default --max-req-timeout of {{max}} seconds. The send still goes: that limit is a daemon flag this app cannot read, so a deployment started with a longer one works and one on the default will answer INVALID_DEFER.

cluster.subtitle: {{nodes}} nsqd, {{directory}} nsqlookupd
cluster.noLookupd: This connection names no nsqlookupd. A single-node NSQ has none, and everything else works without one — add the addresses to the connection to see what the discovery tier is advertising.
cluster.configNote: What this daemon is running with, as it reports itself. nsqd exposes only these — everything else it was started with is a flag it does not report.
cluster.advertiseMismatch: nsqlookupd is advertising {{addresses}}, which this connection cannot reach. Consumers that find their nsqd through discovery are being sent there; check each daemon's --broadcast-address.

clients.search: Filter by client, topic, channel or nsqd
clients.notReady: This consumer has told nsqd it will accept nothing. It is connected and holding its channel, and the backlog will not move until it asks for messages again — usually a handler that has stopped returning.
clients.note: Both roles, from the two places nsqd reports them: a consumer is listed under the channel it subscribed to, a producer under the daemon it is connected to with what it has published. A producer has no ready count and no channel — those are a subscription's. Anything publishing over HTTP is absent, because /pub is a request rather than a connection. One client process appears once per nsqd it found: those are separate connections holding separate messages.

overview.subtitle: {{nodes}} nsqd and {{directory}} nsqlookupd, on {{version}}
overview.undrainedHint: Backlog on channels with no consumer attached
overview.heldHint: Reached no channel: paused, or nothing has ever subscribed
overview.pausedHint: Topics and channels still accepting publishes and delivering nothing
overview.nothingWaiting: Nothing is waiting on any channel.
overview.note: No rate anywhere, and no throughput chart: nsqd counts messages since it started and reports no rate at all. What the tiles separate instead is where the messages are — a backlog with consumers attached is a slow consumer, one with none is a consumer that is not running, and anything held by a topic reached no channel at all.

queues.name: Queue
queues.allInFlight: All {{count}} messages are in flight and none are available — something took them and has finished none of them. They come back when the visibility timeout expires.
queues.note: Every count is approximate: SQS reports what its servers last agreed on. Rates live in CloudWatch, not here.
queues.nameHint: Up to 80 letters, digits, hyphens and underscores. A name cannot be changed afterwards, and SQS refuses it for 60 seconds after the queue is deleted.

nameProblem.tooLong: SQS allows 80 characters, and a .fifo suffix counts towards them.
nameProblem.charset: Letters, digits, hyphens and underscores only — the one dot allowed is the .fifo suffix.

queues.fifoHint: Ordering and deduplication, and a group id on every send. It is decided by the name: turning this on appends .fifo.
queues.fifoFixed: Fixed when the queue was created and spelled in its name. To change it, create another queue and move the messages.
queues.visibilityTimeoutHint: Seconds a received message stays hidden from other consumers. Too short and the same message is handled twice.
queues.retentionHint: Seconds SQS keeps a message nobody deleted. 60 to 1209600 — one minute to fourteen days.
queues.deliveryDelayHint: Seconds every message waits before it becomes available, unless the send sets its own. Up to 900.
queues.receiveWaitHint: Seconds a receive waits for a message. 0 is a short poll, which samples only some of the servers and can come back empty on a queue that is not.
queues.deadLetterQueueHint: The queue failures are moved to, by name. It has to be the same kind — a FIFO queue can only dead-letter into a FIFO one. Leave blank for no redrive policy.
queues.maxReceiveCountHint: Receives before a message is moved to the dead-letter queue. Browsing this app's messages page counts towards it.
queues.contentDedupHint: Deduplicate on the message body rather than on an explicit deduplication id.
queues.purgeDesc: Discards all {{count}} messages the queue holds. SQS purges in the background, so the queue is not empty the moment this returns — and anything sent in the next minute may go with it. One purge per queue per minute is allowed.
queues.deleteDesc: The queue and every message in it go, and there is no undo. SQS refuses the name for 60 seconds afterwards, so it cannot be recreated straight away.

messages.title: Messages
messages.subtitle: Receive from a queue and hand it straight back
messages.receiveNote: SQS has one read, and it is the one a consumer makes: what appears here was hidden from other consumers until it was handed back, and every message's receive count has gone up for good. On a queue with a redrive policy, browsing often enough moves a message to the dead-letter queue with nothing having failed.
messages.startHere: Pick a queue and press Receive.
messages.nothingVisible: Nothing was available. Messages already in flight, still delayed, or on a server this poll did not reach are not returned.

producer.title: Send a message
producer.subtitle: One body, or the same body several times
producer.queueHint: A .fifo name orders its messages and needs a group id on every send.
producer.bodyHint: Up to 256 KB by default, and the queue's own maximum message size can be lower.
producer.countHint: Sends the same body this many times, in batches of ten. Up to {{max}}.
producer.delayHint: Holds the message back from consumers. Up to {{max}} — fifteen minutes is the service's ceiling.
producer.groupIdHint: What this message is ordered against. Messages in one group are delivered in order; different groups move independently.
producer.deduplicationIdHint: SQS treats two sends with the same id inside five minutes as one message and silently discards the second. Leave blank to have one generated.
producer.attributesHint: Named values beside the body, sent as strings. They are the only thing an SQS message carries apart from its payload.
producer.queueRequired: Pick a queue to send to.
producer.groupRequired: A FIFO queue orders messages within a group, so every send needs a group id.
producer.groupOnStandard: Only a FIFO queue takes a group id, and this queue's name does not end in .fifo.
producer.fifoNoDelay: A FIFO queue takes no per-message delay — set a delivery delay on the queue instead.
producer.attributeNameRequired: An attribute value needs a name to be sent under.
producer.fifoRepeatNote: SQS deduplicates a FIFO send on its body for five minutes, so each copy is given its own deduplication id — otherwise all of them would arrive as one message.

dlq.name: Queue
dlq.orphaned: Nothing redrives into this queue any more. Whatever is in it will stay there: the queues that pointed here were deleted or reconfigured, and no consumer of theirs is coming back for it.
dlq.note: Nothing marks a dead-letter queue in SQS — it is an ordinary queue another queue's redrive policy points at, so these were found by walking backwards from the queues this connection can see. Read one on the messages page; the receive limit that fills it is on the queue's own row.

overview.subtitle: {{region}} · {{queues}} queues
overview.queuesHint: In this region, narrowed by the connection's prefix
overview.visibleHint: Waiting for a consumer to ask
overview.inFlightHint: Handed out and not yet deleted
overview.deadLetteredHint: Given up on, and nothing drains it
overview.note: Every count is approximate and comes from the queue listing — the whole of what SQS reports. Rates, ages and per-queue history live in CloudWatch, under a different permission.

topics.name: Topic
topics.noSubscriberNote: Nothing subscribes to this topic, so every message published to it is accepted and then discarded. Nothing downstream records that it happened.
topics.note: A topic stores nothing: a publish reaches whatever subscriptions exist at that instant, and the backlog belongs to each of them.
topics.deleteDesc: The topic goes and its {{count}} subscription(s) do not. They keep whatever they have not delivered, report their topic as _deleted-topic_, and can never receive another message.
topics.nameHint: Three to 255 characters, starting with a letter. A name cannot be changed afterwards: there is no rename call in the API.

nameProblem.tooShort: A name is at least three characters long.
nameProblem.tooLong: A name is at most 255 characters long.
nameProblem.charset: A name starts with a letter and holds only letters, digits and - _ . ~ + %.
nameProblem.reserved: Google keeps names beginning with "goog" for its own resources.

topics.retentionHint: Seconds to keep a published message available for a subscription to seek back into. Zero keeps it only until every subscription has acknowledged it.
topics.retentionRange: Retention is between 600 seconds and 31 days, or zero to leave it unset.
topics.labelsHint: One key=value per line. The whole set is replaced on save, because the API replaces the field rather than one key.

subscriptions.deleteDesc: Everything it has not acknowledged goes with it. Those messages were never the topic's to hand out again, so there is no way back.
subscriptions.name: Subscription
subscriptions.nameHint: Three to 255 characters, starting with a letter. A name cannot be changed afterwards.
subscriptions.topicHint: The one topic it reads, chosen now and fixed: there is no call that moves a subscription to another.
subscriptions.ackDeadlineHint: Seconds a delivered message is held before Pub/Sub offers it again. Between 10 and 600.
subscriptions.retentionHint: Seconds an unacknowledged message is kept. Between 10 minutes and 31 days; the default is seven days.
subscriptions.retainAckedHint: Without this a seek can only skip forward: there is nothing behind the acknowledgement point to go back to.
subscriptions.exactlyOnceHint: The stronger guarantee, which also makes acknowledging something that can fail and be retried.
subscriptions.orderingHint: Delivers messages sharing an ordering key in order. Fixed at creation.
subscriptions.orderingFixed: Fixed at creation. Changing it means a new subscription.
subscriptions.filterHint: A Pub/Sub filter over message attributes, such as attributes.kind = "order". Fixed at creation.
subscriptions.filterFixed: Fixed at creation: the service refuses to change a filter, and so does the emulator.
subscriptions.deadLetterTopicHint: Another topic in this project. Clear it to remove the policy — there is no separate call for that.
subscriptions.maxAttemptsHint: How many attempts before a message is moved to the dead-letter topic. Between 5 and 100.
subscriptions.retryBackoffHint: Minimum and maximum seconds between redeliveries. Both or neither: the service refuses a policy with one.
subscriptions.orphanedNote: Its topic has been deleted, so it will never receive another message. It still holds what it had not delivered, and is still billed for it.
subscriptions.detachedNote: It has been detached, so publishing carries on and nothing is delivered to it. Only an operator can attach it again.
subscriptions.noSnapshots: No restore points on this topic.
subscriptions.snapshotDesc: It copies this subscription's acknowledgement state, not its messages. While it exists the topic keeps everything the restore point could bring back, which costs storage until it is deleted or expires after seven days.
subscriptions.snapshotFailed: Could not take the restore point
subscriptions.snapshotDeleteFailed: Could not delete the restore point
subscriptions.restoreDesc: The subscription starts again from the acknowledgement state the restore point captured. Anything acknowledged since is delivered again, and only as far back as the retention still reaches.
subscriptions.note: There is no backlog column: num_undelivered_messages is a Cloud Monitoring metric, and no call in the Pub/Sub API reports it.

messages.title: Messages
messages.subtitle: Pulled from one subscription. A topic holds nothing to browse.
messages.pullNote: This is a real delivery, not a look. Pull is the only read Pub/Sub has and it is the call a consumer makes: what appears here was held away from live consumers until it was handed back, and every message's delivery attempt has gone up for good. On a subscription with a dead-letter topic, that counts towards being moved there.
messages.startHere: Pick a subscription and pull to see what it is holding.
messages.nothingHeld: This subscription is holding nothing, or a consumer took it first.
messages.noAttemptCount: Pub/Sub counts delivery attempts only on a subscription with a dead-letter topic. This one has none, so there is no count to show.

producer.title: Publish
producer.subtitle: One topic, and whatever subscribes to it at that instant
producer.topicHint: Where the message goes. It is fanned out to every subscription that exists when it arrives, and discarded if there are none.
producer.topicRequired: Pick a topic to publish to.
producer.bodyHint: Sent verbatim. It may be left empty as long as there is at least one attribute.
producer.emptyMessage: A message needs a body or at least one attribute — Pub/Sub refuses one with neither.
producer.countHint: Sends the same message this many times, up to {{max}}.
producer.orderingKeyHint: Messages sharing a key arrive in order — but only on a subscription created with message ordering on. Elsewhere it is carried and ignored.
producer.attributesHint: String key/value pairs beside the body. They are also the only thing a subscription filter can select on.
producer.attributeNameRequired: An attribute with a value needs a name.
producer.noSubscriberWarning: Nothing subscribes to this topic. The publish will be accepted and reported as sent, and the message discarded on the spot.

dlq.name: Dead-letter topic
dlq.noReaderNote: Nothing subscribes to this topic, so every dead letter that arrives is discarded on the spot. The messages a system gave up on are the ones nobody notices disappearing.
dlq.orphaned: No subscription points here any more. It will never receive another dead letter, and whatever it holds is waiting on subscriptions that no longer exist.
dlq.note: A dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic a subscription's policy points at. The policy is on the subscription, so each source names both the topic and the reader that stopped trying.

overview.subtitle: {{project}} · {{topics}} topics
overview.topicsHint: In this project, narrowed by the connection's name prefix.
overview.subscriptionsHint: Each with its own backlog. Two on one topic fall behind separately.
overview.unsubscribedHint: Topics with no subscription. Every message published to one is accepted and discarded.
overview.orphanedHint: Subscriptions whose topic is gone. They hold what they have and will never receive more.
overview.withDeadLettersHint: Subscriptions that give up into another topic after a set number of attempts.
overview.note: No backlog and no throughput here: both are Cloud Monitoring metrics, under a different API and a different credential.

entities.name: Name
entities.noSubscriberNote: Nothing subscribes to this topic, so every message sent to it is accepted and discarded on arrival. It leaves no backlog anywhere.
entities.note: A queue holds its messages; a topic holds none and copies each into every subscription whose rules let it through. Counts come from the entity's runtime properties, which the Service Bus emulator does not report.
entities.deleteQueueDesc: Everything it holds goes with it, its dead letters included — a $DeadLetterQueue belongs to its queue rather than being one of its own.
entities.deleteTopicDesc: This also deletes its {{count}} subscription(s) and whatever they had not delivered. A subscription does not outlive its topic here.
entities.nameHint: Letters, digits and - . _ ~, with / between path segments. It cannot be changed afterwards: there is no rename call.
entities.kindHint: Chosen once. A queue and a topic are different objects at the same path, so changing it would mean deleting one and losing what it holds.
entities.lockHint: How long a receiver holds a message before Service Bus offers it to somebody else. Leave it at 0 for the service's own minute.
entities.lockRange: The lock is between 5 and 300 seconds.
entities.maxDeliveryHint: Deliveries before a message is moved to the dead-letter queue. Leave it at 0 for the service's own ten.
entities.maxDeliveryRange: The delivery limit is between 1 and 2000.
entities.ttlHint: How long a message lives whether or not anything reads it. Leave it at 0 to keep what is set, which for a new entity is fourteen days.
entities.forwardDeadLettersToHint: Another entity to hand this one's dead letters to, which is how several queues' failures are collected in one place. Empty removes it.
entities.fixedAtCreationHint: Both are fixed once the entity exists — the service refuses to change either.

nameProblem.tooLong: A queue or topic name is at most 260 characters.
nameProblem.charset: Letters, digits and - . _ ~ only, with / between path segments.
nameProblem.reserved: A name starting with $ addresses a sub-entity such as $DeadLetterQueue, which has a page of its own.
nameProblem.separator: A / separates path segments, so a name cannot start or end with one.

subscriptions.deleteDesc: Whatever it has not delivered goes with it. A copy that reached this subscription was never {{topic}}'s again, so nothing is handed back.
subscriptions.name: Name
subscriptions.nameHint: Letters, digits and - . _ ~, at most 50 characters. It cannot be changed afterwards.
subscriptions.topicHint: The one topic it reads, chosen once. Moving a subscription would mean a different object with a different backlog.
subscriptions.deadLetterOnRuleErrorHint: A rule whose expression fails to evaluate discards what it was looking at unless this is on.
subscriptions.sessionsHint: Fixed once the subscription exists — the service refuses to change it.
subscriptions.noRuleNote: This subscription has no rules, so nothing can reach it. A new one is created with $Default, which matches everything; deleting that without adding another leaves an object that looks healthy and receives nothing.

nameProblem.tooLong: A subscription name is at most 50 characters.
nameProblem.charset: Letters, digits and - . _ ~ only, and no / — a subscription cannot be nested.
nameProblem.reserved: A name starting with $ addresses a sub-entity such as $DeadLetterQueue, which has a page of its own.
nameProblem.separator: A subscription name cannot start or end with a separator.

subscriptions.note: A subscription is where a topic's messages actually are: each send is copied into every subscription whose rules let it through. Nothing registers as a consumer, so there is no reader count to show.

messages.title: Messages
messages.subtitle: Peeked, not received — nothing here is taken or locked, and no consumer misses it
messages.pickEntity: Pick a queue or a subscription
messages.startHere: Pick a queue or a subscription and peek. A peek takes nothing: the messages stay where they are, their delivery counts do not move, and a running consumer misses none of them.
messages.subject: Subject
messages.scheduledNote: Held back until {{at}}. No consumer is offered a scheduled message, so nothing but a peek would show it.
messages.deferredNote: Set aside by a consumer and reachable only by its sequence number. It will not be offered to anyone until something asks for it by that number.

producer.title: Send a message
producer.subtitle: A queue keeps what it is sent; a topic keeps none of it and copies each message into the subscriptions whose rules let it through
producer.entityHint: Where the message goes. A subscription cannot be sent to — it receives what its topic copies into it.
producer.bodyHint: Sent as it stands. A Service Bus message may be empty, which is how a rule that matches on properties alone is exercised.
producer.countHint: Send the same message this many times, up to {{max}}.
producer.subject: Subject
producer.subjectHint: Also called the label. A correlation filter matches on it by that name, so this is what reaches a filtered subscription.
producer.correlationIdHint: Another field a correlation filter matches by equality.
producer.sessionIdHint: Orders delivery within a session, and is required on an entity created with sessions on. Carried and ignored anywhere else.
producer.delayHint: Schedules the message instead of sending it now. It sits in the entity until its time comes — no consumer is offered it, and the messages page is where it can be seen waiting.
producer.propertiesHint: The sender's own, and what a SQL rule selects on. A subscription filtering on colour = 'red' receives nothing that does not set it.
producer.sentCount: Sent {{count}}. Service Bus assigns a sequence number on arrival and does not report it to the sender — the messages page is where they can be read.
producer.scheduledAs: Scheduled {{count}}, holding sequence {{sequences}} until their time comes.
producer.entityRequired: Choose a queue or a topic.
producer.propertyNameRequired: A property with a value needs a name.
producer.noSubscriberWarning: Nothing subscribes to this topic, so the message will be accepted and discarded on arrival. It will leave no backlog anywhere.

dlq.subtitle: Every queue and every subscription has a dead-letter store of its own, built in and named by the broker
dlq.pickOne: Pick a queue or a subscription
dlq.noEntities: This namespace holds no queues or subscriptions.
dlq.startHere: Pick one on the left. Reading its dead letters is a peek: nothing is taken and nothing is locked.
dlq.nothingGivenUp: Nothing has been given up on here.
dlq.subject: Subject
dlq.forwardedFrom: Forwarded here from {{source}}, which is where it actually failed.
dlq.resent: Sequence {{sequence}} is back on the queue
dlq.resendDesc: It is received from the dead letters, sent to {{entity}} as a new message, and only then removed here. Dead letters are offered in order, so the ones in front of it are read and released — their delivery counts go up, which nothing on a dead-letter store acts on.
dlq.note: A $DeadLetterQueue is part of its entity rather than an object of its own: it cannot be listed, sent to, renamed or shared, and it goes when the entity goes. Reading one takes nothing; putting a message back sends a copy and removes the original.

rules.search: Filter by topic, subscription or name
rules.deleteDesc: {{subscription}} keeps its other rules, so it goes on receiving whatever those let through.
rules.deleteLastDesc: This is {{subscription}}'s only rule. Without one it receives nothing at all — it stays Active and its backlog stays empty, because nothing can arrive.
rules.name: Rule
rules.nameHint: What deletes it: one subscription may have several rules, and nothing else tells them apart.
rules.kindHint: A SQL rule is an expression; a correlation rule compares fields by equality and is cheaper; everything is what $Default is.
rules.expressionHint: Over the message's own fields and the sender's properties, such as colour = 'red' or sys.Label = 'order'.
rules.subject: Subject
rules.subjectHint: The message's subject, also called the label. A correlation filter compares it by equality — no patterns, no operators.
rules.actionHint: Optional. A SQL statement run on a matching message before the copy is placed in the subscription, such as SET routed = 'yes'.
rules.actionNote: This rule changes the message on the way in as well as selecting it.
rules.everythingNote: This rule matches every message on the topic, so the subscription receives all of it whatever else is set beside this.
rules.nothingNote: This rule can never match. It is legal and it is almost never what was meant.

nameProblem.tooLong: A rule name is at most 50 characters.
nameProblem.charset: Letters, digits and - . _ ~ only, and no /.

rules.note: A rule is an object rather than a setting: it has a name, several may sit on one subscription, and each is a filter plus an optional action. A subscription with no rules receives nothing while still reporting itself Active.
